passage:
Transcript: Before there was a census there were parish registers — a clerk writing down each baptism, each marriage, each burial, parish by parish, in a bound book, from the fifteen-thirties onward. A historian who wants a birth rate for the sixteenth century has very little else to work from. And the trouble with these books is not that the clerks were careless. It is that a burial register records a funeral, and a funeral is something a parish decides to hold.

Think about an infant who lives two days. In a great many parishes such a child went into the ground without a service and without an entry. Nobody was hiding anything. The book was simply not kept for that event. So the registers undercount infant deaths, and they undercount them by an amount nobody can observe directly, because the entries that would tell you are the entries that are not there.

Halloran has found a way at it. She works in parishes where a second and independent list happens to survive — a sexton's fee book, say, which records the digging rather than the service, because the digging was paid for. In the eleven parishes she has assembled the fee books carry between twelve and thirty per cent more infant burials than the registers do. Her conclusion is that the shortfall is real, that it is large, and that it is roughly uniform: correct every parish upward by a fifth, she says, and the national series becomes usable.

Now, I accept the eleven parishes. A fee book listing graves that the register does not list is about as direct as this kind of evidence ever gets, and I have no quarrel at all with the measurement.

What I do not accept is the second half of it — the roughly uniform. A sexton's fee book survives where a parish was rich enough to pay a sexton and orderly enough to keep his accounts. Those are precisely the parishes least likely to have been casual about the register in the first place. So the eleven are not eleven draws from England. They are eleven draws from the tidy end of England, and whatever they establish about the size of the shortfall, they cannot tell you how it varies.

And the variation is the whole problem. A shortfall that is a fifth everywhere raises the level of infant mortality and leaves every comparison between parishes standing. A shortfall that is a fifth in Devon and a half in the northern uplands rearranges the map. Halloran's method works in the parishes where it can be applied, and those are not the parishes where the answer would matter.
prompt: [Academic Talk — Historical Demography] What did Halloran find in the parishes where a register and a sexton’s fee book both survive?
choices: More infant burials in the fee books than in the registers, by twelve to thirty per cent.
The same infant burials in both records, with about a fifth of them dated a year apart.
Fewer infant burials in the fee books than in the registers, by roughly a tenth.
More infant burials in the fee books, the gap widening from a twentieth to a third across the century.
correct_answer: More infant burials in the fee books than in the registers, by twelve to thirty per cent.
explanation: The lecturer gives the comparison as a count of infant burials and puts the excess in the fee books at between twelve and thirty per cent, which is the figure the proposed one-fifth correction is drawn from. The excess is given as a single range across the eleven parishes, not as a trend and not in the other direction.

distractor_rationales.choice: The same infant burials in both records, with about a fifth of them dated a year apart.
distractor_rationales.reason: The one-fifth in the talk is the size of the correction Halloran proposes, not a proportion of entries dated differently; the two lists differ in which burials they contain, not in when they place them.

distractor_rationales.choice: Fewer infant burials in the fee books than in the registers, by roughly a tenth.
distractor_rationales.reason: The direction is the wrong way round. The fee book records the digging, which happened whether or not the parish held a service, so it is the fuller list rather than the thinner one.

distractor_rationales.choice: More infant burials in the fee books, the gap widening from a twentieth to a third across the century.
distractor_rationales.reason: The direction is right and the trend is invented. The talk reports a single range across eleven parishes and never puts the excess on a course over time; a widening gap would be a different finding with different consequences.

passage:
Transcript: An ancient coin was struck between two dies — a lower die holding the blank, an upper die brought down with a hammer. A die is a hand-cut block of iron, and it wears, and it chips, and it cracks, and every flaw it picks up is printed onto every coin it makes afterwards. Which means a hoard can be sorted. These forty coins came off one obverse die; these twelve came off another. Sorting is slow, it is done by eye, and it is the closest thing this field has to a laboratory.

Once a hoard is sorted you can count the dies in it. The hoard from the well deposit I keep coming back to holds eleven hundred and forty coins and sixty-three obverse dies, and seventeen of those dies are represented by exactly one coin. Those seventeen are the interesting ones, because a die that shows up once is a die you very nearly missed, and the number of dies you very nearly missed is what tells you how many you missed altogether. From there you estimate the total the mint cut. Multiply the total by the coins one die could strike, and you have the city's output in money.

Ivers is the person to read on that multiplier, and she is devastating about it. Experimental strikings put the output of a single die anywhere from a few thousand to several tens of thousands, depending on the alloy, on how hot the blank was, on how hard the smith hit it. A range of that width is not a figure. I agree with her. I do not think that number is recoverable from anything we have, and I would not print an output in coins for any ancient city.

But watch what survives. Suppose I am not asking how much the city struck, and I am asking instead whether it struck more than its neighbour. The same unknown multiplier enters both estimates, and in the ratio it cancels. I do not need to know it; I need only to be confident that it is the same on both sides, which requires the two mints to have worked the same metal in the same way. Ivers thinks that condition fails even between one generation and the next inside a single city, and there we part company.

One caution before you try any of this yourselves. A die that cracks halfway through its working life prints two versions of the same flaw, before the crack and after it. Sort your coins by flaw rather than by die and you will count that one die twice, and every estimate downstream of the count will be too large.
prompt: [Academic Talk — Numismatics] Why, on the lecturer’s account, can a comparison between two mints survive an unknown output per die?
choices: Because the same unknown figure enters both estimates and drops out of the comparison.
Because the comparison works from the number of dies directly and never converts it into coins.
Because an error in the figure pushes both estimates in the same direction by the same number of coins.
Because the figure matters only for mints small enough to have worked with a handful of dies.
correct_answer: Because the same unknown figure enters both estimates and drops out of the comparison.
explanation: The lecturer says the multiplier cancels in the ratio and that what is needed is not its value but confidence that it is the same on both sides — which is why the argument then turns on whether the two mints worked the same metal in the same way. That condition would be pointless if the quantity were unused or if it merely shifted both totals equally.

distractor_rationales.choice: Because the comparison works from the number of dies directly and never converts it into coins.
distractor_rationales.reason: If the comparison never used the multiplier, the lecturer would not need the two mints to share a metal and a technique, and that requirement is the thing Ivers attacks.

distractor_rationales.choice: Because an error in the figure pushes both estimates in the same direction by the same number of coins.
distractor_rationales.reason: A shared multiplier acts on each estimate in proportion to its own die count, not by an equal number of coins; an equal shift would not leave a ratio unchanged.

distractor_rationales.choice: Because the figure matters only for mints small enough to have worked with a handful of dies.
distractor_rationales.reason: Nothing in the talk makes the multiplier a small-mint problem. It enters every conversion of dies into coins, which is why the lecturer will not print an output for any city.

Transcript: Birds in cities sing higher than birds of the same species in the countryside. Not by a great deal — the bottom of the song lifts by a few hundred hertz — but it has been measured in enough species and enough cities that the pattern is not in doubt. What is in doubt is what it means.

The first account is the one you will meet everywhere. Traffic is a low sound. Almost all of its energy sits below about two kilohertz, underneath where these birds do their singing, and a song with its lowest notes lifted clear of that band carries further through a city than one that sits down in it. On this account the bird is doing something about the noise, and the pitch of its song is the thing it is doing.

The second account says the pitch rise is a by-product and nothing more. Any vocal animal sings louder in a loud place; that reflex is old and it is not about frequency. And in a songbird the loudness and the pitch of a note are not independently controlled. The membrane has to be held tighter to sing louder, and a tighter membrane vibrates faster. You cannot raise the one without raising the other. So on this account the bird is responding to how loud the city is, not to where the city's energy sits, and the pitch would have gone up even if traffic noise were a hiss at eight kilohertz.

Naunton has now recorded both quantities in one species along a gradient from a quiet park to a ring road, and loudness and pitch rise together, and they rise together tightly. I have seen the data and I believe it.

I want you to notice that it does not help us. The adaptive account expects a bird that is working to be heard to sing both louder and higher. The by-product account expects pitch to follow loudness because it has no choice. Both accounts predict Naunton's correlation, and a measurement that both sides predict is not evidence for either of them. I am not going to tell you which is right, because I do not know.

I will tell you what I would do. Take birds into an aviary and play them a noise of a kind traffic does not make — loud, but all of it above the song rather than below it. If the bird is working around a masking band it should now move its song down, away from the noise. If the loudness reflex is doing the work it should sing louder and therefore higher, as before, and go straight up into the interference.

choices: That almost all of its energy sits below about two kilohertz, underneath the song.
That almost all of its energy sits above about two kilohertz, over the top of the song.
That its energy is spread evenly from about one to about eight kilohertz.
That its energy moves upward in frequency as the traffic gets heavier.
correct_answer: That almost all of its energy sits below about two kilohertz, underneath the song.
explanation: The first explanation has the bird lifting the bottom of its song clear of a band of interference, which only works if the interference is a band and is below the song. That is why the lecturer’s proposed test uses a noise that traffic does not make — one placed above the song instead.

distractor_rationales.reason: Noise above the song is the artificial case the lecturer reserves for the aviary test; if real traffic were like that, raising the song would move it into the interference rather than clear of it.

distractor_rationales.choice: That its energy is spread evenly from about one to about eight kilohertz.
distractor_rationales.reason: Evenly spread noise leaves nowhere for a song to move to, so an account built on escaping a band would have nothing to work with.

distractor_rationales.choice: That its energy moves upward in frequency as the traffic gets heavier.
distractor_rationales.reason: The explanation turns on where the energy sits, not on its moving; a noise band that climbed with the song would defeat the strategy it is supposed to explain.

Transcript: The seeds of the cycad are a good food. They are also poisonous, and not mildly so; the compound in them attacks the nervous system. Communities that live on them process the seeds first, and the processing is elaborate. The kernels are cut and soaked, the water is changed on a schedule, the material is rinsed in a set order, it is left to stand for a period that is not negotiable, and only then is it dried and ground. Days, not hours.

The standard account of how such a sequence arises is straightforward and, I think, wrong. On that account somebody worked it out. People noticed that the seeds made them ill, noticed that soaking helped, noticed that longer soaking helped more, and assembled the steps the way you would assemble any technique, each step kept because it was seen to do something.

Perrin has spent years with communities that do this, and what she found does not look like that. The sequence is taught as one unbroken order, start to finish, and a step is not treated as a thing with a reason of its own. When she asked why a particular step was done she got no reason at all, or she got a reason that is simply wrong about what is in the seed and what removes it. And the sequence contains steps that do nothing. One of the rinses, in the order it is given, removes no more of the compound than the rinse before it, and the standing period could be halved with no measurable effect. Those inert steps are guarded exactly as carefully as the long soak, which is the step doing nearly all of the work.

I follow Perrin here, and I would add the reason I find decisive. The illness this food causes is not an illness you get at dinner. It appears after years, sometimes after decades, as a slow failure of the nerves in the legs. Nobody eating these seeds could ever have watched a shortened preparation make somebody sick, because the sickness does not arrive while anyone is watching. The link that the standard account asks an individual to notice is a link that no individual is in a position to notice.

What is left, then, is a sequence that travelled whole. Communities that performed all of it, including the parts of it that do nothing, are the communities that are still here to be recorded, and that is a different kind of selection from anybody's insight. So if you meet a village that has taken up cycad seeds recently, my expectation is not a lean version of this with the useless steps filed off. It is the whole thing, carried over entire.

Answers that differed from one household to the next, with no two accounts agreeing.
Answers that placed the step within living memory, as something recently taken up.

Transcript: Leave a rock sitting on a desert surface for long enough and it goes dark. What forms on it is called rock varnish: a coating of clay minerals a few micrometres thick, stained by manganese and iron that airborne bacteria concentrate out of the dust that settles on it. It builds slowly and it builds only where nothing disturbs the surface, which makes it, on the face of it, a clock. A thick coat means an old surface. I said a moment ago that thickness gives you an age for a boulder field or an alluvial fan, and I am going to come back to that.

First, Sedgemoor's work, because it is the best thing in this field. Take a chip of varnish, section it, and put it under the microscope, and the coating is not uniform. It is layered — dark bands and orange bands, tens of them, each a few tens of nanometres. The dark bands form in wetter intervals and the orange in drier ones, and because the climate they record is regional, the pattern of bands in one section can be matched against the pattern in another, site to site, the way you match rings between two timbers.

Now, back to what I said at the start about thickness giving an age. I want to take that back. It is not that thickness records nothing; it is that what it records is not a duration on its own. The coating grows at a rate set by how much dust arrives and how often the surface is wetted, and those two things are local.
